Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
- 58-y-o woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presents with 5-day history of dry cough and profuse green rhinorrhoea; clinical impression is an acute viral upper respiratory tract infection/bronchitis with advice to monitor for bacterial super-infection.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Dry cough every 20–30 min and constant nasal discharge began abruptly 5 days ago.
- Associated symptoms: Subjective fever with alternating chills, myalgias, transient diarrhoea at onset (resolved). Denies sputum, haemoptysis, chest pain, dyspnoea, wheeze, sore throat, ear pain, headache, visual change, rash, vomiting, current diarrhoea, urinary change.
- Pertinent negatives: No prior chronic lung disease, no regular chest infections.
- Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypertension.
- Medications: Metformin (dose not stated); Lisinopril (patient believes “200” mg, likely 20 mg); PRN Lemsip (contains paracetamol 2–3 sachets/day).
- Allergies: No known drug allergies; mild seasonal hay-fever.
- Social / preventive: Lives with partner and dog; office manager; denies smoking; occasional sherry. No home glucose monitoring; routine diabetes blood tests “normal” 3 wks ago.

Examination:
- Remote video consult; no vitals obtained.
- Patient appears well; no reported dyspnoea, chest pain, or focal sinus tenderness.

Impression:
- Most likely: Acute viral upper respiratory tract infection / viral bronchitis (supported by abrupt onset, cough, rhinorrhoea, myalgias, subjective fever, absence of alarming chest features).
- Alternative considerations:
  • Early bacterial sinusitis or lower-respiratory super-infection (green discharge, diabetes as risk factor) – monitor.  
  • COVID-19 infection (symptom overlap; no anosmia reported).

Plan:
- Symptomatic care: Continue Lemsip (contains paracetamol); avoid other paracetamol-containing products.
- Purchase thermometer; check temperature regularly.
- Safety-net advice: Seek review if temperature ≥ 37.5–38 °C persists or spikes, worsening cough, development of purulent sputum, haemoptysis, shortness of breath, chest pain, or new focal symptoms.
- Possible antibiotics or further evaluation if above red-flags occur.
- Night-time cough syrup permissible only if cough prevents sleep; avoid daytime use.
- Chronic disease follow-up: Ensure regular diabetes and blood-pressure reviews with GP; advised to arrange home blood-sugar monitoring.
- No immediate investigations or prescriptions issued today.

Quality checks:

● Missing / expected elements:
  – Objective vitals (temp, HR, RR, BP, O2 sat).  
  – Clarified smoking status (patient did not answer).  
  – Exact medication doses, vaccination status (influenza/COVID), recent BP readings, glucose logs, allergy confirmation.  
  – Formal follow-up timeline not specified.

● Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  – DDx raises ACE-inhibitor cough; transcript timing favors infection (no management conflict).

● Transcript quality:
  – Generally clear; occasional inaudible words and incomplete social history; remote setting limits physical exam data.
